sections.body_en:
A woman from whom nidda blood (the blood of a menstruant) has emerged, that is, the blood of the veset (menstrual period), has become impure, and the man and the woman have become forbidden to each other, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): "And when a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days." The nidda blood that renders impure is the blood that comes out of the womb, as it is stated (Vayikra 20:18): "And if a man lies with a woman in her infirmity (nidda)… and she has uncovered the source of her blood (she consented to the union while the blood was coming out of her womb) – both of them shall be cut off from among their people." That is to say, the womb, in which life is formed, is also the place from which the impure blood of nidda and ziva comes out. Through the mitzva of ona (marital relations) during the days of purity and the prohibition of closeness during the days of nidda, the man and the woman strengthen the bond between them in a way that adds goodness and life, and they refrain from diverting their powers toward the side of impurity and evil, which destroy and cut off their lives.

Blood has various colors: there are shades that are pure and there are shades that are impure, as it is stated (Devarim 17:8): "If a matter of judgment is too hard for you, between blood and blood" – "between pure blood and impure blood" (Nidda 19a). The Sages learned from the precise wording of the verses that the Torah intended to forbid four shades of blood, and that the other shades of blood are pure. These are the impure ones: 1) 'Red like the blood of a wound' – like the blood that comes out of a cut immediately after the injury, and not a little while afterward. 2) 'Like a crocus stalk' – like the thin leaves of saffron, whose color is red-orange. 3) 'Like earthy water' – like the color of fertile soil in the valleys of the Galilee when flooded with water, whose color is brown-red. 4) 'Like mazug' – like the color of red wine from the Sharon that was mixed with a double quantity of water (red-purple). 5) The Sages further said that there is a fifth color – black like ink, which is in fact the first color of blood, 'red like the blood of a wound', whose color has deteriorated and changed (Nidda 19a–20a). By Torah law, all the other shades of red, black, pink, orange and brown are pure.1

notes_en.en:
Mishna Nidda 19a: "Five types of blood are impure in a woman: red, black, like a crocus stalk, like earthy water, and like mazug (diluted wine)." The Gemara explains that the five bloods were learned from the fact that "the source of her blood (dameha)" is stated twice in this context (Vayikra 12:7; 20:18) in the plural, implying that there are four types of blood, and the black is red that has deteriorated and turned black. Tosafot Ha-Rosh explains (Nidda 20a, s.v. 've-khulan') that the Sages established these five bloods because they are the ones commonly found in a woman, and it stands to reason that these are the ones the Torah forbade. Further on, the Mishna explains that Beit Shammai are stringent regarding two more shades, and Akavya ben Mahalalel is stringent also regarding a type of green that is yellow like an egg yolk, and the halakha does not follow them. These four shades of blood are not on a single scale of red, one darker than the other; rather, they are different shades, each with its own scale of lightness and darkness. Therefore the Gemara disputes the law of each of the shades when it is slightly darker or slightly lighter, and it is agreed that a much lighter or much darker shade is pure. And there are many other shades of red that are not impure (Binat Adam 8:13; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 188:5).
All the impure bloods are impure on condition that they came out of the womb, but if they did not come out of the womb – they are pure. As the Sages explained in the Mishna (Nidda 17b): "The blood of the ḥeder (the womb) is impure; the blood of the aliya (some say the ovaries and some say the urinary bladder) is pure." However, not all the bloods that come out of the womb are impure, for as explained above, pure bloods also come out of the womb (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 5:6). It is possible that some of the shades of pure blood are the discharges that come out before the start of the veset or after it. That is to say, sometimes the uterine lining, from which the menstrual blood comes out, breaks down in a longer and more gradual process, and since at first a little blood is discharged that is diluted in other fluids, it has no impure color; likewise, at the end of the breakdown the percentage of blood decreases until it no longer has an impure color. (According to the Ra'avad, most bloods from the makor (the uterus) are impure, and this is why they said in Nidda 21a: 'The opening of the womb is impossible without blood.' By contrast, according to the Razah, it is possible that most bloods are not impure, as we learned from Rabbi's decree above, 1:6.)
As a general rule, one can perhaps say that the impure bloods are those that come out in a process of loss of life, such as the nidda period, in which the egg and the lining that could have sustained the fetus are lost, and ziva, in which the process of forming the egg and the lining is impaired. But bloods that come out without harming the life that is meant to take shape in the womb, or that come out after the life that had begun to form has already been lost – are not impure.

sections.body_en:
Distinguishing between impure blood and pure blood requires great expertise, because the shades of blood are many, and one must become accustomed to observing their color and texture in order to distinguish between the forbidden and the permitted. Therefore the Torah instructed us to ask the Sages in cases of doubt, and in rare cases even to ask the Great Court in Jerusalem, as it is stated (Devarim 17:8): "If a matter of judgment is too hard for you, between blood and blood" – "between pure blood and impure blood" – "then you shall arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose," to hear the instruction of the Sages as to which shade is of pure blood and which shade is of impure blood. Therefore they were also careful not to examine bloods at night, so that they would be able to discern the exact color of the blood (Megilla 14a).

For example, the first shade is "red like the blood of a wound." The Sages explained (Nidda 19b) that this means the blood that comes out of an ox immediately after its slaughter, and not the blood that comes out of it afterward. They further said that it is like the blood of a head louse and not like the blood of a body louse, whose color is slightly different. They further said that it is like the blood of a wound of a young man and not of an older person. And all this was to explain the first shade. Similarly, the Amoraim disagreed about all four shades of red when they had changed to become slightly darker or slightly lighter. Similarly, the Sages said in the Mishna regarding black blood that it is like ink, and they explained that if it is less deep, for example if it is black like a raven or like pitch – it is pure (Nidda 20a).

In the wake of the destruction of the Temple and the dispersion of the exiles, the traditions weakened, until even eminent rabbis had difficulty distinguishing between impure and pure bloods. Thus it is related about three of the greatest Amoraim, Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi, that they went to have blood let, following the medical recommendation that was accepted in those days. After the blood began to flow into the first vessel, Ameimar, who was the eldest of the group, said that this blood is of the color of 'blood of a wound,' which is the first type of impure blood. Afterward, when the blood flowed into the second vessel, he said that this blood is no longer like the blood of a wound, and therefore it does not render forbidden. Rav Ashi, who was Ameimar's disciple and colleague, said that he could not distinguish between these shades of blood, and therefore he could not rule on them (Nidda 20a). Over time, many Sages refrained from distinguishing between shades of impure blood and pure blood, and were stringent to declare them all impure, until in the period of the Rishonim it was already agreed throughout Israel to be stringent regarding all the red and black shades of blood.2

notes_en.en:
The Rosh wrote (Nidda 2:4): "In these generations there is no one expert in the appearances of blood, such that one could rely on his wisdom and distinguish between blood and blood; and even in the days of the Sages of the Talmud there were some Sages who refrained from examining them. All the more so nowadays, one must not declare pure any blood that tends toward a reddish appearance, unless it is white, or green like the appearance of gold." So wrote the Ra'avad, Or Zaru'a, Ramban, Ran, Eshkol and SA (YD 188:1): every red appearance, whether dark or light, is impure. Likewise a black appearance is impure. Only an appearance that has no redness, even if it is thick like blood, is pure.
Some have written that ever since Rabbi's enactment and the acceptance by the daughters of Israel of 'the stringency of Rabbi Zeira,' they also became stringent regarding all shades of blood, and so it emerges from the Rif (Shevuot 3b), the Rambam according to the Maggid Mishneh (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 11:11), and the Tur at the end of 183 (Sugah Ba-shoshanim 191:3; see Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 188:2, and Berur Halakha 188:2). But it is difficult: according to their view, how could Ameimar, who lived several generations after Rabbi Zeira, still rule leniently regarding some of the shades of blood? One may answer based on what is explained in Nidda 66a, that the stringency of Rabbi Zeira was accepted gradually, and in Ameimar's place it had not yet been accepted. It seems more likely that even according to the stringency of Rabbi Zeira one may rule on the shades of blood, but as a continuation of the idea at the basis of his stringency – to make the laws uniform in order to prevent confusion – the stringency not to distinguish between impure and pure blood was gradually accepted, until in the period of the Rishonim it became binding halakha.

sections.title_en: Between the Impure and the Pure Colors
sections.body_en:
Although it was agreed to forbid all the red shades of blood, the task of halakhic ruling still requires study and experience in order to distinguish between an appearance that has the redness of blood and an appearance that does not have the redness of blood. This is especially difficult when the appearance dries out, and the redness in it fades and its color changes. Seemingly, one could solve the problem by defining the colors by their names: the forbidden ones are red, red-pink, burgundy and black, and the permitted ones are yellow, gray and brown; and indeed many poskim wrote so. However, this definition is insufficient, because there are countless shades and combinations of shades, and many of the colors of blood may be in intermediate shades. And if we try to define the permitted and the forbidden according to the names of colors, sometimes we will forbid the permitted and permit the forbidden. Defining the color of blood as the red color familiar to us is also inaccurate, because generally the color of blood while it is still moist tends more toward burgundy, and after it dries its color changes in the direction of purple or brown. The intermediate colors close to red and black, such as purple, brown, pink, orange and gray, are also sometimes forbidden and sometimes permitted. The definition closest to the halakha is that if the intermediate shades have the redness of blood, that is, something like the burgundy or purple color of blood – they are forbidden, and if they do not have these shades – they are permitted.

In practice, one learns to distinguish between an appearance that has blood in it and an appearance that does not have blood in it by becoming accustomed to seeing the blood of the veset, and the shade in which it appears when moist and when dry. When it is clear to the woman that the appearance has the reddish color of blood – it is impure. And when it is clear to her that it does not have the reddish color of blood – it is pure. And if she is in doubt – she should ask a Torah scholar. It is worth noting that there are women in whom the process of the cessation of bleeding is gradual, and toward its end there are impure brown-red appearances, which gradually turn into pure brown ones.3

notes_en.en:
In the ancient languages, including the Hebrew of the days of Ḥazal, only a few colors had names, such as black, white, red and green, and the other colors were included in them. In Hebrew, the color 'red' also included brown, burgundy, pink and purple; the color green included yellow and blue; the color black included all the very dark colors, and the color white all the very light colors. When they needed to be precise in defining a color, they generally said that it is like the color of a certain thing in nature, as the Sages defined the five colors of the impure bloods (above, note 1). Only toward the modern era did the languages develop, and abstract names were created for additional shades of color. Therefore, when Akavya ben Mahalalel (Mishna Nidda 19a) disagreed with the Sages and said that green blood is impure, he meant yellow like an egg yolk or gold, which sometimes have a slight tinge of redness. Similarly, we find in Scripture and in the words of the Sages that brown is called red, as they said, for example, that horses are red (Zekharia 1:8; Bekhorot 6a, and Rashi there), whereas in fact they are brown with a tendency toward redness (see the article by Rav Azarya Ariel in Ma'alin Ba-kodesh 33, and Dr. Nadav Shnerb in Teḥumin 23).
As a general rule, the poskim wrote that if the appearance has shades of red – it is impure, and if yellow or golden – it is pure (SA 188:1). However, in the name of the Maharam Mintz they wrote to be stringent regarding yellow like wax or gold, and according to the Shela one should be stringent regarding them if they came out with a sensation. However, the vast majority of poskim were lenient regarding them. They further disagreed regarding brown like coffee or like chestnut shells: according to Beit Meir 188:2 and Beit Shlomo YD 2:4, it is forbidden. But many permitted it, among them She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:44, Sidrei Tahara 188:1, and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 9. Some say that even according to the stringent opinions, if the color is like coffee with milk – it is pure (Levushei Mordekhai 1:111). Some leaned toward stringency in bedikot, the internal examinations for purity (Simlat Binyamin 10; Shevet Ha-levi 188:1). Some were stringent regarding dark yellow in the hefsek tahara, the examination establishing that bleeding has ceased (Ḥokhmat Adam 117:9, and Darkhei Tahara 3:4 leaned toward this). By contrast, the overwhelming majority of poskim hold that there is no need to be concerned about yellow even in the hefsek tahara (Maharsham, Da'at Torah 188:1). They similarly disagreed regarding orange, pink and gray. It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the disputes over the shades of colors are narrow, for if the brown has redness, as some types of coffee and chestnuts do, it is agreed that it is forbidden, and as we learned, in the past they called this brown "red." And if the brown has no redness, like other types of coffee – it is permitted. The dispute concerns a certain shade of brown that lies in between and has a slight tendency toward redness. The same applies to orange, pink and yellow. In practice, as I wrote above, defining the names of colors is not very helpful; the main thing is to become accustomed to seeing the blood of the veset while it is moist and after it has dried, in order to distinguish between its color and the color of other discharges, and this is indeed the practice when one studies how to rule on appearances (mar'ot). It should be noted that in practice today, in most cases where an appearance has a black color, its source is external and not from the womb, and therefore it does not render impure (Orot Ha-tahara 2:12).

sections.body_en:
The impure blood that comes out of the womb renders the woman impure by Torah law on condition that it came out with a sensation (hargasha), in the way that the menstrual blood of nidda comes out. But if it came out without a sensation, even if it is known with certainty that it came out of the womb and its color is like the color of the impure bloods, it does not render impure, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): "And when a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood." The Sages explained: "'In her flesh' – until she feels it in her flesh" (Nidda 57b). This law was stated for nidda and for zava (a woman with a non-menstrual flow) alike (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 9:1).

One can explain that the impurity is generated by blood coming out of the womb in a process that involves a loss of vitality, a kind of death. For if it came out in the framework of nidda, then an egg that could have developed into a fetus has been lost. And if in the framework of zava, then a problem has arisen in the very process of the formation of the egg and its implantation in the womb. And it is the nature of the body that such blood, of loss of vitality, comes out with a sensation; therefore blood that came out without a sensation does not render impure.

However, the Sages decreed impurity also on a ketem (bloodstain) that came out of the womb without a sensation, if it meets three conditions: 1) the stain was more than two centimeters in diameter; 2) it is on a white background; 3) it is on something that is susceptible to impurity. But if the stain was not more than two centimeters, or was not on a white background, or was not on something susceptible to impurity – it does not render impure. This is because at the time when the laws of purity were observed in Israel, blood that came out of the womb without a sensation, even though it did not forbid the woman to her husband, was itself impure and rendered impure the pure items (taharot) it touched. Therefore the Sages decreed that whenever it renders pure items impure, it should also forbid the woman, on condition that the three aforementioned conditions are met. The Sages further said that whenever there is a doubt in the laws of ketamim (stains), one should be lenient, as Rabbi Akiva said (Mishna Nidda 58b): "For the Sages did not state this matter in order to be stringent – but rather in order to be lenient."4

notes_en.en:
The impurity of nidda and zava by Torah law applies only when the blood came out with a sensation, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): "And when a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood" – "blood, and not a ketem" (Mishna Nidda 58b). And if it came out without a sensation, under certain conditions the Sages decreed that it be impure by the law of ketem. Thus we learned in Nidda 57b: "Shmuel said: If she examined the bare ground and sat on it, and found blood on it – she is pure, as it is stated 'in her flesh' – until she feels it in her flesh." It is explained from the words of Rav Ashi that the woman is pure because the blood came out without a sensation and onto something that is not susceptible to impurity, like the ground; but blood that came out onto something that is susceptible to impurity renders impure by rabbinic law, by the law of ketem (the words of Rabbi Akiva and of Shmuel are consistent, as explained in Responsa Shev Ya'akov 36; Arukh La-ner, Nidda 58a).
Some say that if it is known with certainty that the blood came out of the womb, even without a sensation – she is impure by Torah law (Sidrei Tahara 190:93, explaining Rashi and several other Rishonim). However, the overwhelming majority of poskim hold that it is a scriptural decree that only if the blood came out with a sensation does it render impure by Torah law, and if not, even though it is clear that it came out of the womb – by Torah law it is pure. So wrote Responsa Maharam of Lublin 2; Pardes Rimonim; Ḥokhmat Adam; Tzemaḥ Tzedek YD 97. And they proved this likewise from the words of the Rambam, Ramban, Or Zaru'a, Rashba, Ran, Kol Bo, Haggahot Maimoniyot, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and Tur.
The basis of the decree of ketamim rests on the fact that even blood that came out without a sensation is impure by Torah law, and therefore it renders impure anything that is susceptible to impurity, such as a garment or a vessel. Since this is so, the Sages decreed that the woman from whose womb the blood came out should also be impure. Therefore some hold that since the laws of purity lapsed, the decree of ketamim also lapsed, and they do not render a woman impure nowadays (as the Eshkol inferred from the Rif, Behag and She'iltot, who did not mention the law of ketamim). However, the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim hold that ketamim render a woman impure nowadays as well, for the Sages did not annul their words. Indeed, some explain that the decree of ketamim is also based on the concern that perhaps the woman felt a sensation and did not pay attention (Rashi). However, from the words of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim as a whole it emerges that the basis of the prohibition of ketamim rests on the laws of purity, and therefore when the blood came out onto something that is not susceptible to impurity – the stain is pure (Tosafot Nidda 58a, s.v. 'ke-Rabbi'; Rashba in the name of his teacher Rabbeinu Yona, Ran and Meiri on Nidda 57b; Ḥatam Sofer, Nidda 58a; Sho'el U-meshiv Kamma 1:153; Hit'orerut Teshuva 3:22; and similarly in Noda Bi-Yehuda Kamma YD 52).
[Many explained that blood that came out without a sensation is impure only according to the view of the Tannaim who hold 'the makor (source, i.e. the uterus) – its place is impure,' meaning that blood that comes out of the womb renders impure with regard to pure items, and this is the accepted halakha (Rambam, Hilkhot Metam'ei Mishkav U-moshav 1:9; 4:15, and most Aḥaronim). So wrote Sidrei Tahara 190:93, s.v. 've-od re'aya'; Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥavot Da'at, Mareḥeshet and others. From their words it is implied that according to the view of those who hold 'the makor – its place is pure,' the Sages did not decree regarding ketamim, or the decree was not on account of the laws of purity. However, according to the Ra'aviya, the halakha follows the view of those who hold 'the makor – its place is pure,' and nonetheless a stain found on something susceptible to impurity forbids; and Rabbi Akiva Eger (Kamma 62) and Igrot Moshe (YD 4:14) explained that according to their view the Sages decreed regarding ketamim because whatever they said about 'its place is pure' concerns blood that came out not in its normal way, such as from the wall of the womb, inside a piece of tissue, or after the woman's death; but they too agree that nidda blood that came out without a sensation renders pure items impure, and therefore the decree of ketamim is needed.]

sections.body_en:
As we have learned, the sensation (hargasha) that accompanies the emergence of blood is very significant for halakha: if the blood came out with a sensation, even a tiny drop of it renders impure. And if it came out without a sensation, it renders impure only if the blood formed a stain more than two centimeters in diameter on a white object that is susceptible to impurity.

The Sages of the Talmud, the Ge'onim and the Rishonim did not explain what this sensation is; rather, they related to it as a known and familiar sensation that needs no explanation. However, in recent generations there has been uncertainty about the definition of the sensation that women feel when the blood comes out, and from their words as a whole three explanations emerge. 1) Some inferred from the precise wording of the Rishonim and the Talmud and explained that the sensation is a kind of opening of the womb, or a kind of sensation of a shudder and a shiver. The problem is that many women have stated that they do not feel such sensations when the blood comes out. Seemingly, according to this, they do not become impure by Torah law during their veset, but this cannot be, for it is not reasonable that the Torah law of nidda and zava has been nullified for them. It also cannot be that nature has changed so much that sensations that were known to all women have disappeared.
2) Some say that the feeling of blood flowing from the vagina is also considered a sensation, and this is a sensation that many women feel during their veset. 3) Some say that general bodily sensations that precede the appearance of the veset or accompany it are also included among the sensations that make the blood render impure by Torah law. But it is still difficult, for we learned from the words of the Mishna and the Talmud that there were women who felt the moment the veset began, and there were those who could feel it even in the middle of relations (Shevuot 14b). Whereas the sensation of blood flowing from the vagina and the general bodily sensations do not characterize the moment the veset begins, nor can they be felt in the middle of relations.5

notes_en.en:
Several of the great Aḥaronim derived definitions of the sensation from the precise wording of the Rishonim. From the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 5:17) they learned that sometimes the blood comes out with a shudder and a shiver, like the passing of urine. From Terumat Ha-deshen 246 they learned that it refers to a feeling that the mouth of the womb has opened to release blood, and so it is cited in SA 190:1. Some learned from the Gemara (Nidda 3a) that it refers to a feeling that involves discomfort, and that is why there were women who woke from their sleep because of it. Some explained that it refers to a slight discomfort, like the discomfort felt when the need to urinate arises, from which a sleeper also wakes (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 183:60). And perhaps it refers to emotional distress due to the awareness that the blood is beginning to flow, to soil and to render impure. After all this, when women were asked what the sensation of the emergence of blood is, they had difficulty explaining it. The Maharshashakh (d. 5479/1719) wrote that he asked women and they explained that each woman has her own nature and sensation: some feel a strong sensation as if "something is falling from the mouth of her source," and some feel only the flow of something moist. And sometimes one woman feels one such sensation at one time and another sensation at another time (cited in Shev Ya'akov 39). The Noda Bi-Yehuda (YD Kamma 55; d. 5553/1793) explained that it refers to the feeling of blood flowing from the vagina, which is a feeling that women feel during the veset. And although other Aḥaronim agreed with this (Maharshashakh, Ḥokhmat Adam, Beit Meir and Beit Shlomo), most poskim disagreed and held that since this feeling is noticeable only when the blood is already in the vagina, it cannot be the sensation that renders impure, for the woman already becomes impure when the blood comes out of the womb into the vagina (Penei Yehoshua YD 1; Shev Ya'akov 40; Ḥatam Sofer YD 145, and others). Some explained that the feeling of the flow of something moist forbids on condition that she felt its passage from the womb into the vagina (Ḥavot Da'at 190:1; Tzemaḥ Tzedek, Avnei Nezer and others). Some learned from the women's answers that the vast majority of them do not feel the emergence of the blood from the womb (Tiferet Tzvi 190:14, d. 5563/1803; Teshurat Shai YD 457). Some say that in truth women today also feel the opening of the makor (source), but they do not know how to define it (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 183:61–62; Igrot Moshe YD 4:17:12). And some say that the senses have weakened, and therefore they do not pay attention to these subtle sensations (Divrei Yatziv YD 87:6; Shevet Ha-levi 10:142).
The third explanation is that the sensation that forbids includes all the sensations that accompany the veset before its appearance and at the time of its appearance, and not necessarily at the moment the blood comes out. This can be inferred from the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 9:1), who wrote: "until she feels and sees blood and it comes out in the flesh, as we have explained," and the only place where he explained the sensation is regarding a bodily veset, where he wrote (ibid. 8:1–2): "There is a woman who has a veset… and before the blood comes she feels it in herself: she yawns and sneezes, and feels pain at the opening of her abdomen and in her lower belly, and the hair of her flesh bristles, or her flesh grows warm, and similar occurrences…" This is the view of Shev Ya'akov 40; Sidrei Tahara 190:1; Pardes Rimonim, Pitḥei Nidda 4; Maharam Schick 177, 182, 184; Tzitz Eliezer 6:21; Igrot Moshe YD 4:17:12.

sections.body_en:
From the discussion as a whole, and according to most opinions, it emerges that the sensation of which the Sages spoke is not one particular feeling, but rather a range of feelings that accompany the veset, which in different women are expressed in different ways. However, the rule is that the woman knows clearly from her feelings that menstrual blood is coming out of her. And one should not be surprised that it is difficult to define the feeling of the emergence of menstrual blood, for all bodily feelings that involve various components in the body, such as hunger, tiredness and pain, are difficult to define. This is because they comprise a whole fabric of different feelings that take shape in each person's consciousness in a unique way, and still all people know what is meant. Similarly, the sensation of the emergence of menstrual blood, which stems from a hormonal process that affects the woman's entire body, is perceived through a range of bodily feelings, such as headaches, abdominal pains, heaviness in various limbs, nervousness, irritability, low spirits to the point of a tendency to cry, shivering, the opening of the womb and the flow of blood from the vagina. Some women are very precise in discerning their feelings, to the point that from among all the feelings they can discern the subtle feeling of the opening of the womb, or a shiver when the uterine lining begins to break down and come out as bleeding. Some feel a general sensation that their veset is about to arrive, and as a result, when they feel something moist flowing from them, they know with certainty that it is menstrual blood. And there are women who are less attentive to all these feelings, and only in the midst of the veset, when much blood is flowing from them, does a certain feeling that menstrual blood is coming out of them take shape in their consciousness.

In the past, more women felt the moment the menstrual blood began to come out, perhaps because the appearance of the veset had a great effect on their way of life, and the alertness in anticipation of it sharpened their senses to feel its emergence more. However, even then there were women who did not feel the beginning of the bleeding, and therefore the Sages decreed that a woman who saw blood must be concerned about pure items she touched during the preceding twenty-four hours, lest her blood had already begun to come out then. In any event, the possibility never arose that women who did not feel the moment the veset appeared did not become impure by Torah law, because it was clear that ultimately every woman feels the veset at the very least when it is in full course.

Therefore, even though the precise sensation of the opening of the womb and the beginning of the emergence of blood has become somewhat dulled, the rule of halakha has not changed: every woman who knows clearly from the feelings of her body that menstrual blood is coming out of her becomes impure by Torah law, and it makes no difference from which combination of feelings she knows this. And whenever she does not know that she is bleeding because of the veset, the law of the blood she sees is like the law of a ketem, which is impure only under certain conditions.6

notes_en.en:
From the fact that the Talmud and the Rishonim did not deal with defining the sensation, one can learn that it is not one particular sensation, but rather, like the other feelings of the body, a combination of varied feelings that are perceived and take shape in each woman in a unique way. The main point for halakha is that from the feelings of her body the woman knows that menstrual blood is coming out of her, and this awareness needs no explanation, for it is clear to all. There is indeed a difference between women: the most sensitive felt, from among all the feelings, the moment of the opening of the womb at the beginning of the emergence of blood; the less sensitive felt some shudder from the separation of the blood from the womb, and knew in a general way that the blood was about to come out; and the even less sensitive could know with certainty that they were in the midst of the veset only when much blood was flowing from the vagina (Binat Adam 7:7 wrote something similar). But it cannot be that there would be women who become forbidden by Torah law without feeling it and being able to take care not to stumble in forbidden matters, for the ways of the Torah are ways of pleasantness, and it would not establish prohibitions in which people would stumble (Responsa Shev Ya'akov 1:36; Beit Yitzḥak YD 2:15:3; Ḥatan Sofer 53:1).
Indeed, a change has also taken place in sensitivity to feelings: in the past more women felt the opening of the womb, whereas today there is almost no woman who feels it. Apparently, in the past the appearance of the veset had a greater effect on women's ways of life, many of whom were accustomed to withdraw during those days to the inner rooms of their homes. This was both because of the laws of purity, for from the moment she became impure, every food, vessel or garment she touched became impure; and because of hygiene, for at a time when there were no undergarments or pads available, there was embarrassment when the blood began to flow. And just as the blind are able, by means of their hearing, to discern subtle sounds that the sighted do not perceive, in order to compensate for their lack of sight, so women in the past were more attentive to the combination of feelings that accompanied their veset, in order to compensate for the absence of a solution for absorbing the blood as it came out, to the point that some of them could pinpoint the moment the blood appeared. It is also possible that over the generations, the focus on thoughts and emotions has increased at the expense of the focus on perceiving bodily feelings in all their variety. However, even in the past there were women who did not feel the moment the veset appeared, and therefore the Sages were stringent to forbid pure items they touched during the preceding twenty-four hours, unless they examined themselves within that time and did not see blood (Mishna Nidda 2a). Apparently, the preoccupation with explaining the sensations arose in the days of the Aḥaronim because of two factors: first, attentiveness to bodily feelings became somewhat dulled over the generations; second, it is the way of the Aḥaronim to define precisely what was understood in a general way by the Rishonim.
In practice, the bodily sensation that generates impurity by Torah law is the sensation that forms in the woman the awareness that the blood coming out of her is coming out in the framework of a veset, and it makes no difference on the basis of which feelings exactly that awareness took shape. So it emerges from the words of Rashi (3a, s.v. 'margeshet'): "that is, she knows in herself when blood comes out of her." So wrote Beit Meir 188:4. Similarly, Pardes Rimonim wrote (General Introduction, Inquiry 1:5) that when the bloods come out in the manner of a veset, she is impure by Torah law. (So I heard in a shiur from Rav Ovadia Yosef, and so wrote Minḥat Asher, Nidda 1.) According to this, the Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not disagree about the definition of the sensation; rather, they wrote different descriptions of the sensation: the opening of the mouth of the makor, or a shudder, or general feelings as written by the proponents of the third explanation (in the previous note).
As we shall see further on in the chapter, this general explanation fits the ruling of the poskim: on the one hand, even today a stain found on white undergarments does not forbid by Torah law, since it came out without a sensation, and there is no concern that perhaps she felt a sensation but does not know what the sensation is. On the other hand, women who do not feel a particular sensation of the opening of the mouth of the makor or a shudder during their veset, but saw that a large quantity of blood came out of them, like the quantity of a veset – since the awareness has formed in their minds that this blood is menstrual blood, they are impure by Torah law even if all of their seeing was on a colored garment or on something that is not susceptible to impurity.

sections.title_en: The Size of a Forbidden Ketem
sections.body_en:
The Sages established that a stain whose size is the measure of a geris or less does not render impure, because up to this size it was possible to attribute the blood of the stain to a large louse that had been crushed unawares; but if the stain is larger than a geris, it is already clear that it came from the body. A geris is a large bean split in half, and in our measurements it is the area of a circle with a diameter of 2 cm.

Even today, when lice from which blood the measure of a geris could come out are not found in homes, and it cannot be claimed that a stain the size of a geris came from a louse, one should not forbid a stain whose measure is a geris or less. This is because by Torah law any blood found without a sensation does not render impure, and it was the Sages who decreed impurity on stains, and their decree was only on a stain of more than the measure of a geris. Moreover, many explained that their enactment was chiefly with regard to pure items, and in connection with this they extended their decree also to the prohibition of closeness between a woman and her husband; and even after the destruction, when the laws of pure items lapsed, their decree did not lapse, but one should not extend it beyond what they decreed (above, note 4).

If several stains were found on the garment, none of which is more than a geris, but together their measure is larger than a geris, they do not combine to forbid, for only a single stain of more than 2 cm renders impure. If there was a thick stain of a size that does not render impure, but had it spread over the garment it would have been of a size that renders impure – since in fact it did not spread, it is pure.7

notes_en.en:
It is explained in Nidda 58b that Tannaim in the Mishna and the Gemara disagreed regarding stains: according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, only if the woman killed a louse and afterward found a stain of a size that could be from that louse is she pure. By contrast, according to the Sages, even if she did not kill a louse or a bedbug, as long as the stain is up to the size of the blood of a bedbug (which is much larger than a louse), she is pure. And Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonos holds an intermediate view: even if she did not kill a louse, as long as the stain is up to the size of a 'geris' (a split bean), she is pure. The Amoraim disagreed whether exactly the size of a geris renders impure, and the ruling is lenient: the size of a geris bean is pure, and more than that renders impure (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 9:23; SA 190:5). In practice, it is accepted to rule that a geris is the area of a circle with a diameter of 2 cm, and more than that renders impure (Me'il Tzedaka 27; Ḥatam Sofer; Taharat Ha-bayit 8:2; Otzar Ha-halakha 190:33).
Some are stringent and hold that if there are no lice in the house whose blood is the size of a geris, one may be lenient regarding a stain only up to the size of the blood of the lice that are found there and no more. And if no lice at all are found in that place, one may not attribute it to them at all (Rav Shlomo Kluger, Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at Telita'ah 2:75; Rav Pe'alim 1, YD 36). Some say that if the color of the stain was black, since it cannot come from a louse, it is impure even if smaller than a geris (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 190:9; Teshurat Shai Tinyana 142). And many poskim hold that whenever there is a doubt whether the stain came out of the womb, even in a house with no lice one should be lenient according to the law of stains; but when there is certainty that the stain came out of the womb, even if it is smaller than a geris, if it came out onto a white object that is susceptible to impurity, it renders impure (Pleti 183:1; Sidrei Tahara, Ḥavot Da'at, Binat Adam, Pardes Rimonim, and in our day Ḥut Shani and Shevet Ha-levi).
By contrast, many are entirely lenient and hold that since at the time the Sages decreed regarding stains, lice were commonly found in homes, the Sages established their decree according to their size, and did not decree regarding less. And even when there is certainty that the stain came out of the womb, as long as it is not more than the size of a geris regarding which the Sages decreed, since it came out without a sensation, it is pure, and one should not add further decrees on our own initiative (Me'il Tzedaka; Torat Ha-shelamim; Ḥatam Sofer YD 150; 182; Maharam Schick). We already learned in note 4 that the decree was chiefly on account of pure items, and although the laws of pure items lapsed, the decree did not lapse; but one should not add to what they decreed. In practice, since the prohibition of stains is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient view, and so ruled Igrot Moshe YD 3:46; Taharat Ha-bayit 8:2.
Two stains do not combine to make up the measure, and even if there was a thin line connecting them, they do not combine, since it is evident that they are two stains (Responsa Tzemaḥ Tzedek YD 144; Yabi'a Omer 8, YD 16:2). But a single stain whose two impure parts are separated by pure shades – since it is one stain, if its impure shades together amount to the measure, it is impure (Me'il Tzedaka 62). A thick stain that could have spread over more than a geris – since in fact it is not of the measure, it is pure; for otherwise we would have to distinguish between whether it is on a thick or a thin garment, and the Sages fixed their words and did not leave them to [varying] measures (Sidrei Tahara 190:61; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 34). Therefore, even if because of its great quantity it passed through two garments, and on neither of them is there the measure, the two garments are not combined to make up the measure (Paḥad Yitzḥak and Ikarei Ha-dat). If there was a stain on a white garment and it was lost or laundered by mistake, and a doubt arose whether it was of the measure that renders impure or whether it was of a color that renders impure – since the law of stains is rabbinic, one should be lenient (Ḥokhmat Adam 113:29; Rav Shlomo Kluger; Divrei Malkiel and others).
Some say that if the stain was found on the woman's body, it forbids even if less than the measure of a geris (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 9:6; Shakh). Some say that it does not forbid if less than a geris, but two stains on the body combine to make up the measure (Ra'avad, Ramban, Ran, Sidrei Tahara, Ḥokhmat Adam, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, and in our day Taharat Ha-bayit 8:3). And some are lenient, holding that the law of stains on the body is like the law of stains on a garment, and several stains are not even combined to make up the size of a geris (Rabbeinu Yona, the unattributed opinion in SA 190:8; and in our day Darkhei Tahara 2:16 leaned toward this). And this is the halakha.

sections.title_en: A Ketem on a Colored Garment
sections.body_en:
If the stain is found on something colored, such as colored underwear, even in a light color, there is no prohibition in it. This is because by Torah law any blood that came out without a sensation is permitted, and when the Sages forbade stains, they forbade them on condition that it is possible to discern whether they are of the color of impure blood or of pure blood. And since on something dyed, even if it is light, it was not possible to discern the fine difference between impure and pure blood, they did not forbid stains on colored garments.

If the stain was found on a white garment that has colored patterns or stripes on it, what is on the color does not combine, and only if the stain on the white part is more than the measure of a geris is it impure.

In order to avoid impurity from stains, it is proper for a woman to take care to wear colored underwear during her days of purity (Rambam; Rema 190:10). Indeed, during the shiv'a neki'im (the seven clean days) it is a proper custom to wear white (Rema 196:3). But a woman who is concerned that she may see stains because of wounds, or an intrauterine device, or hormonal pills and the like, should wear colored underwear even during the shiv'a neki'im, since there is no obligation to wear white (as explained below, 4:9).8

notes_en.en:
Nidda 61b: "The Rabbis taught: A dyed garment renders impure on account of a ketem. Rabbi Natan bar Yosef says: It does not render impure on account of a ketem, for colored garments were enacted for a woman only to make things lenient regarding her stains. Enacted? Who enacted them? Rather, colored garments were permitted to a woman (among the decrees following the destruction they forbade garments in joyful colors, and then permitted them again) only to make things lenient regarding her stains." The Ramban ruled stringently like the first Tanna, and the Dagul Me-revava (190:10) took his view into account. By contrast, the Rambam, Rosh, Eshkol, Meiri and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam were lenient, and so it is ruled in the Tur and SA 190:10. The Ḥatam Sofer (YD 161) was stringent regarding a garment that is tight against the body. However, the overwhelming majority of poskim were lenient (Teshuva Me-ahava 1:163; Rav Shlomo Kluger, Maharsham and others). And this is the halakha, in keeping with the rule that in the laws of stains the halakha follows the lenient view, all the more so when they are the majority.
The Aḥaronim wrote that all shades of color are included in a colored garment (Me'il Tzedaka 62; Ḥokhmat Adam 113:9; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 190:23). Some say that if the color is very light, it is considered as white, and a stain on it forbids (Shevet Ha-levi 2:87). However, many are lenient even regarding a very light color (Tzitz Eliezer 6:23:9; Taharat Ha-bayit 8:6). And this is the halakha, for the basis of the permission of stains on a colored garment is that at the time when they distinguished between impure blood and pure blood, when there was an additional shade they could no longer distinguish between them, and consequently, when the Sages decreed regarding stains, they did not decree regarding a garment with color (Responsa Beit She'arim 261; Ḥeshev Ha-efod 2:92).
If there were colored stripes on the white garment, one calculates the stain that is on the white area, and one even combines two parts on both sides of the colored stripe, and it does not separate between them as long as it is evident that it is a single stain (Me'il Tzedaka 62; Ḥokhmat Adam 113:10; Pitḥei Teshuva 190:20; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 44; unlike the Ḥavot Da'at and those who agree with him, who were stringent to count the colored part as well).
A woman who sees blood not during her veset days because of taking hormonal pills to prevent pregnancy, whether while nursing or not while nursing, cannot attribute this bleeding to a wound, and therefore its law is like that of any blood: in an internal bedika it renders impure in any amount, and in an external sighting it is subject to the law of stains (Darkhei Tahara 7:106). In order to avoid becoming impure, it is customary to instruct women who take pills to wear colored underwear and to minimize internal bedikot. (However, Minḥat Shlomo 2:73:1 was uncertain whether bleeding resulting from taking pills renders impure.)

sections.title_en: A Ketem on Something Not Susceptible to Impurity
sections.body_en:
If the stain was found on something that is not susceptible to impurity, such as on the toilet bowl or on the bathtub, then even though it is clear that the stain is blood that came out of the womb, it is not impure. For the entire basis of the decree of stains is that the stain rendered impure the thing onto which it came out, and the Sages decreed that in connection with this it should also render the woman impure, even though she did not feel its emergence. But if it does not render impure the thing onto which it came out, there is no reason to decree that it should render the woman impure.

As a rule, garments and vessels are susceptible to impurity, whereas raw materials from nature are not susceptible to impurity. A panty liner, a sanitary pad, cotton wool and toilet paper are not susceptible to impurity, because they are made of materials that are not susceptible to impurity. And even if they were made of cloth, since they are intended for one-time use, they are not susceptible to impurity.9

Some are stringent and hold that a stain on something not susceptible to impurity or on a colored garment does not render impure on condition that it is not very large; but a very large stain, such as 7 cm by 7 cm, renders impure, lest it be blood that came out with a sensation and she did not pay attention to it. By contrast, some are lenient and hold that as long as the blood came out without the sensation of a veset, even if the garment is entirely soiled with blood, its law is like that of a stain that does not render impure, on a colored garment or on something not susceptible to impurity. In practice, many are accustomed to be stringent, especially during the shiv'a neki'im. Those who wish to be lenient may do so, as long as it is clear that the blood did not come out in the framework of a veset.10

notes_en.en:
Mishna Nidda 59b: "Rabbi Neḥemya says: Anything that is not susceptible to impurity is not susceptible to stains." And there in the Gemara (60b): "The Sages ruled in accordance with Rabbi Neḥemya." We have already learned in halakha 4 and note 4 that the decree of stains is based on the laws of pure items: since even blood that comes out of the womb without a sensation renders impure the thing onto which it came out, they decreed that it should also render the woman impure; but when it came out onto something not susceptible to impurity, it consequently does not render the woman impure. [Some forbid a stain even on something that is susceptible to impurity only by rabbinic law (Noda Bi-Yehuda YD Tinyana 109; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 41), and some are lenient (Pri De'a; Divrei Ḥayim YD 2:80; Or Same'aḥ). And the rule in the laws of stains is to be lenient.]
Nidda 60b: "Abaye said: Rabbi Neḥemya would declare pure rags that do not measure three by three (fingerbreadths), since they are of no use to either the poor or the rich." That is, the minimum size of a cloth for it to be susceptible to impurity is three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths. This is for a woolen or linen cloth, but for other cloths the measure is 3 tefaḥim by 3 tefaḥim; and if it was prepared specially for use, even if it measured only 3 fingerbreadths, it is susceptible to impurity (Rambam, Hilkhot Kelim 22:1; 21). Three fingerbreadths are 5.7 cm; three tefaḥim are about 23 cm.
Cotton wool is not considered cloth and is not susceptible to impurity (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 183:2; MB 629:12). Likewise, toilet paper is not susceptible to impurity (Rambam, Hilkhot Kelim 2:1; Igrot Moshe YD 3:53). Some were stringent regarding pads and panty liners, since they become subsumed into the underwear (Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv; Mishmeret Ha-tahara 3:14), and some were stringent regarding them since they have been processed and have thereby become like a vessel (Darkhei Tahara 2:20–21, and in the accompanying responsa). However, many were lenient, because the materials from which they are made (petroleum, plastic and nylon) are not susceptible to impurity, and because pads and panty liners are not fit for reuse (Taharat Ha-bayit 8:9–11; Be-ohalah Shel Torah 1, YD 25; Minḥat Asher 2:62). In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view, both because their reasoning seems correct and because in a dispute in the laws of stains one should be lenient.

In principle, blood that came out without a sensation onto a colored garment or onto something not susceptible to impurity, even if it is very large, does not render impure, for the measure of more than a geris was stated only for a situation in which it renders impure; but in a situation in which it does not render impure, even a larger one, without limit, does not render impure. So wrote the Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit Ha-katzar 7:4): "And even if it is entirely soiled with blood, she need not be concerned." And so wrote Tzitz Eliezer 6:23:12, that one who is stringent regarding a stain because it contains much blood goes against the words of the poskim. So also wrote Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 1, p. 413; Badei Ha-shulḥan 190:108; Orot Ha-tahara 3:17. Ḥut Shani 190:12–13 was lenient like the Rashba regarding a very large stain on something not susceptible to impurity, but was stringent regarding a thick stain on a colored garment, since it is clear from its color that it is blood. Some leaned toward stringency from a size of three geris (Avnei Shoham 190:1). Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv and Shevet Ha-levi (10:142–143) also leaned toward stringency, but they did not write from what size one should be stringent. And in the name of Rav Moshe Feinstein they wrote in Mesoret Moshe (vol. 3, p. 224) that one should be stringent regarding a stain the size of half a dollar bill (about 6.6 by 7.8 cm).

sections.title_en: Doubt Whether the Blood Came from the Womb
sections.body_en:
A stain of more than the measure of a geris on a white garment renders impure on condition that it is known to have come out of the womb, for example if it is found on the underwear. And if she was not wearing close-fitting underwear, it renders impure when it is found on a white sheet or on a white nightgown and it is clear that it came out of the womb. But if there is some doubt that perhaps the stain came from another place and not from the womb, even though in all likelihood it came from the womb, it does not render impure. For since it came out without a sensation, by Torah law it is pure, and the Sages were stringent regarding it on condition that it is clear that it came from the womb. And so Rabbi Akiva said (Nidda 58b): "For the Sages did not state this matter in order to be stringent – but rather in order to be lenient, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): 'And when a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood' – blood, and not a ketem."

Therefore, if there is a possibility that the stain found on the underwear was formed by blood that came out of a wound in her body, she is pure; and even if the wound has scabbed over, as long as there is some chance that the wound opened and the blood came from it, she is pure. Likewise, if there is a possibility that the stain came from hemorrhoids, or from a urinary tract infection, or from bowel movements due to an upset stomach, or from eating beets and the like, she is pure. Likewise, if there is a possibility that the stain came about because she touched chicken or fish blood, or beets, or lipstick, or a red marker and the like with her hands, and afterward stained her underwear with her fingers, she is pure. And even when the chance of this is small, as long as there is some chance that the stain came from another source that is not her womb, she is pure.11

notes_en.en: In the past people were not accustomed to wearing underwear, and then, if the stain was found on her body or on her garment in a place that blood from the womb could not reach, she is pure, and in a place that it could reach from the womb, she is impure, as explained in Nidda 57b; SA 190:11–14. This is on condition that there is no possibility that it came from another source; but if it is possible that it came from another source, such as a wound of hers or of members of her family, or the blood of an animal or a bird, she is pure, as explained in SA 190:16; 18–19. Likewise, if blood comes out of her husband's urethra, and she found blood after relations, she may attribute the blood to him (ibid. 190:20). Various laws are likewise explained as to when there is a chance that the blood came from another source and she is pure, and when there is no chance and she is impure (ibid. 190:21–22). The law depends also on the color of the stain and its size: if she handled a small amount of a bird's blood or killed a louse, and the stain is larger than the amount of blood she handled or its color is different, she is impure; and if it may have come from it, she is pure (ibid. 190:7; 23–30). Further laws are cited in the Talmud and in the SA, and they relate to the living conditions of the past; the rule is that whenever there is a chance that the blood did not come from the womb, she is pure.

sections.title_en: The Law of an Internal Bedika and of Wiping after Using the Toilet
sections.body_en:
If she examined herself deep in the vagina, then even if the bedika was done with a colored cloth that is not susceptible to impurity, and she found a small amount of blood, like a mustard seed, she is impure. For since it was found deep in the vagina, near the opening of the womb, we are concerned that perhaps it came out with a sensation, now or in the preceding hours, and then it forbids by Torah law, and consequently the leniencies of stains do not apply to it. Blood found on a tampon is also considered like blood found in an internal bedika.

If she wiped herself after using the toilet and found blood on the toilet paper: some are stringent and hold that since it is clear that the blood came out of the vagina, there is reason to be concerned that it came out with a sensation and the feeling of passing urine dulled the sensation. Therefore, in their opinion, it is preferable that she not look at the toilet paper in the first wipings. But in practice, even though the blood certainly came out of the vagina, since in fact it was absorbed outside the vagina and she did not feel its emergence, its law is like that of a stain, and since it is on toilet paper, which is not susceptible to impurity, she is pure. Likewise, if she wiped with a colored cloth, she is pure. Likewise, if she wiped with a white cloth that is susceptible to impurity, but the stain was not more than the measure of a geris, she is pure.12

notes_en.en:
The poskim disagreed in explaining the Gemara in Nidda 57b. According to the lenient view, even when the woman thinks that she felt blood come out of her womb, if this sensation was after passing urine, or an internal bedika, or relations, her sensation is attributed to these actions, and the blood is treated according to the law of a stain. This is the plain meaning of the Gemara, and so wrote Maharam of Lublin 2; Neta Sha'ashu'im YD 21; Tzemaḥ Tzedek YD 98–99; Leḥem Ve-simla 183:2; and they based their words on Rashi and on the Maharam of Rothenburg cited in Haggahot Maimoniyot (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 4:20). By contrast, some explained that the Gemara deals with cases in which the woman did not feel the emergence of blood from the womb, but since these actions – passing urine, an examination with an ed (examination cloth), and relations – dull the sensation, when it is likely that the blood came from the womb, the blood she found is regarded as blood that came out with a sensation, and one is stringent regarding it even when it is less than a geris, and on a colored garment, and on something not susceptible to impurity. So wrote Kreti U-pleti 183:1; Shev Ya'akov 36; Ḥavot Da'at 190:1; Binat Adam 7:8; Rabbi Akiva Eger Kamma 62; Ḥatam Sofer in his novellae on 183; and so they learned from Tosafot and the Rashba. Likewise in our day Shiurei Shevet Ha-levi 183:4; Ḥut Shani 190:10; and Igrot Moshe YD 4:17:13; 16 leaned toward this. And there is an intermediate view: in an internal bedika, even if the woman is sure that she did not feel the emergence of the blood, one is stringent; but in an external examination, even after urine or relations, the law of the blood is like that of a stain. So wrote Pardes Rimonim; Sidrei Tahara 190:36; Har Ha-mor 20; Maharal Tzintz, Meshivat Nefesh 30; Malbushei Tahara. And so wrote in our day Tzitz Eliezer 6:23; Ḥeshev Ha-efod 2:151. And so I wrote above. (See Taharat Ha-bayit 1:5; Yabi'a Omer 8, YD 16; 9, OḤ 107:1.)
Seemingly there is a profound dispute between the two polar opinions, as to whether blood found in an internal bedika or after passing urine or relations is considered blood that came out with a sensation or not. In practice, however, the dispute is narrow, for even the stringent opinions concede that if the blood is found when wiping or on the underwear about half a minute after actions that may dull the sensation, its law is like that of a stain, even though she cannot vouch that she did not feel a sensation. For it is explained in Mishna Nidda 14a, and in the Gemara there 14b; 15a, that the entire stringency of regarding blood after relations as rendering impure by Torah law applies when it is found 'otiyom,' that is, within the time sufficient for an external wiping immediately after relations and no more. And if she found the blood a little afterward, she is impure out of doubt. And if after that, she is not impure, and they decreed only with regard to pure items. Therefore, even those who are stringent regarding blood found in an external examination after urine or relations are stringent only within about half a minute to a minute (Shiurei Shevet Ha-levi 190:10:3). And they are stringent when she did not wipe around the area; but if she wiped around the area, some doubt is added that perhaps the blood came from another place, and then its law is like that of a stain (Igrot Moshe YD 4:17:13; 16; Ḥut Shani p. 409). On the other hand, the lenient opinions also agree that if the blood is found in a bedika deep in the vagina, as long as she cannot determine with certainty that she did not feel a sensation, the law of the blood she found is like that of blood that is impure by Torah law. As explained in the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 5:5), if the blood is found in a bedika deep in the vagina, it is presumed to be from the womb, "and one is liable on its account for entering the Sanctuary, and teruma and sacrificial food are burned on its account. And we do not say that perhaps it came down from the aliya through the opening, for most bloods found here are from the ḥeder (womb)."
That is to say, the principle is that any blood found without a sensation is forbidden by rabbinic law according to the law of a stain, and only in an internal bedika is one stringent to regard it as having come out with a sensation, even though in fact she did not feel a sensation. Some explain the reason for the stringency in an internal bedika as being that perhaps the bedika dulled the sensation (Pleti 183:1), and some explain that perhaps a little blood came out earlier and she did not pay attention (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 183:54). But it is difficult: if it is a matter of concern, why is one stringent regarding blood found in an internal bedika as if it were certain? It seems that on top of the fundamental rule that only blood that came out with a sensation renders impure by Torah law, since there are situations in which the sensation is unclear, the Sages established, on the basis of a presumption (ḥazaka), an additional boundary: any blood found deep in the vagina, as long as there is no wound or other thing to which to attribute it, is presumed to have come out with a sensation. And perhaps one can say that the Torah law of the sensation applies to a situation in which the blood is found outside the vagina, regarding which the Sages learned "her discharge in her flesh is blood" – "until she feels it in her flesh" (Nidda 57b). But when the blood is found actually in her flesh, that is, precisely in the place where the process of impurity takes place, then "her discharge in her flesh is blood" has been fulfilled in the most tangible way, and she is impure by Torah law even without a sensation. Rabbeinu Ovadia stated something similar to this interpretation (Responsa Maharaḥ Or Zaru'a 112; and see Mishmeret Ha-tahara 1:4, note 16).

sections.title_en: Doubt Whether She Felt That the Veset Began
sections.body_en:
A woman who felt a clear sensation that menstrual blood is coming out of her must examine herself in order to know whether she has become impure, and in the meantime the couple must refrain from contact. This examination need not be internal, with an examination cloth (ed bedika); rather, it is sufficient for her to do an external examination at the opening of the vagina with toilet paper. If she saw blood in her examination, even a very small amount, she is impure. And if she did not find blood, she is pure.

And if she is in doubt whether she felt a clear sensation of the emergence of menstrual blood – for example, usually after such a sensation a veset begins, but there have been cases in which after such a sensation the veset did not begin – when she feels this sensation, she must examine herself with an external examination, and in the meantime the couple are forbidden to have relations. If in the examination she finds blood in an amount from which she knows that her veset has begun, she has become impure. And if she does not find blood, she knows that she is pure without doubt. And sometimes she will find a little blood, and since the blood was found in an external examination, its law is like that of a stain that does not render impure. However, if as a result of the stain she found a doubt arose in her mind that perhaps the veset is about to begin, then even though she did not become impure from the stain, she should refrain from relations until the end of the ona (by day – until sunset, and by night – until sunrise). And if during the ona her veset does not begin, she is pure.

If she felt a sensation after which most of the time she does not find menstrual blood, she need not be concerned about it; she remains in a presumptive state of purity and need not examine herself. Likewise, a woman who at the time of ovulation felt a sensation similar to the beginning of a veset, and afterward found only a drop of blood – since it has become clear to her that this sensation is not that of the beginning of a veset, the law of the blood she found is like that of a stain that came out without a sensation.13

notes_en.en:
In principle, from the moment a woman has felt with certainty that her veset has begun, even if she has not actually seen blood, she is presumed impure and is forbidden to her husband in relations and in touch. As we have learned (Shevuot 14b; 18a; SA 185:4), a woman who felt in the middle of relations that she had become impure – her husband must withdraw with a "dead organ," that is, without an erection, and if he did not do so, he is liable to karet. Thus, on the basis of a certain sensation the woman is presumed impure; and so wrote Ḥakham Tzvi 46; Pleti 183:1; Leḥem Ve-simla 185:6; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 32.
Similarly, a woman who felt that her makor opened for the emergence of menstrual blood: according to Terumat Ha-deshen 246, even if she examined herself and found nothing, she is impure, for presumably blood came out and was lost or dissolved, since a complete sensation has the force of Torah law. By contrast, according to the Radbaz 1:149 and She'ilat Ya'avetz 2:5, if she examined herself and found nothing, she is pure, because only a sensation together with a sighting is forbidden by Torah law. The SA (190:1) and most Aḥaronim leaned toward the stringent view of Terumat Ha-deshen. But many wrote that the stringency is due to doubt and not certainty, both because perhaps pure blood came out and perhaps she was mistaken in her sensation (Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana 118; Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at Telita'ah 2:64; Yehuda Ya'aleh YD 220), and because this law is the subject of a dispute (Divrei Ḥayim 1, YD 37). Therefore, the entire stringency applies only to a certain sensation of the opening of the makor, which Terumat Ha-deshen mentioned (Ḥokhmat Adam 113:1; Taharat Ha-bayit 7:1). In addition, if she was wearing underwear, there is no longer a concern that the impure appearance was lost, and if she did not find blood, she is pure (Badei Ha-shulḥan 188:22; and see Rabbi Tzadok Ha-kohen of Lublin in Responsa Tiferet Tzvi 2:1:14).
In any event, we have learned that in both topics, according to the stringent view, which is that of most of the Aḥaronim, after a certain sensation she must examine herself. And it seems that even most of the lenient opinions would agree to this, for even though a sensation alone does not forbid, nevertheless, since a great doubt has arisen, it should not be ignored, and she must examine herself. However, since the poskim did not mention an obligation of a bedika in this matter as they mentioned it for the shiv'a neki'im and the ona of the veset, an external examination to see whether the veset has begun is sufficient.
Sometimes, on the basis of her sensations, the woman is in doubt whether her veset has begun, and then, because of the doubt, she must examine herself with an external examination. However, since she is not sure of her sensation, if she finds blood, its law is like that of a stain. Indeed, it is possible that as a result of finding the stain she will become more confident in recognizing her sensation, and will know that her veset has begun. And it is possible that even after seeing the stain she will remain in doubt; and although she did not become impure because of it, for example because it was on a colored garment, nevertheless, since a significant doubt has arisen, she must separate according to the law of separation near the veset. And if the ona passes and the veset does not begin, the doubt is resolved and they are permitted to have relations. And a woman who knows that many times these sensations do not herald the veset for her need not examine herself (see Rav Shlomo Kluger, Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at Telita'ah 2:65; Darkhei Tahara 1:13).

sections.body_en:
The blood that renders impure is the blood that comes out of the womb in the framework of the menstrual cycle or of ziva; but blood that comes out of a wound in the vagina, and even from a wound in the womb, does not render impure. There are three situations in this law: 1) When it is clear to the woman that the blood came out of the wound. 2) When it is clear that there is a wound that can release blood, but it is doubtful whether the blood that was found came out of it. 3) When it is doubtful whether there is a wound that releases blood.

1) The Sages said that a woman is believed to say, "I have a wound in that place that releases blood," and then the blood that came out from there does not render her impure (Nidda 66a; SA 187:5–6). Some women know that the blood comes from a bleeding wound because of a feeling of the pain of a wound in the vagina close to the appearance of the blood; some know it because they examined the vagina and felt with their finger the wound that releases blood; and some reach this conclusion because they saw that the blood came out mixed with pus, unlike menstrual blood. Likewise, a woman who examines herself with an internal bedika and finds that the blood always appears on the same side can conclude that she has a wound on that side (SA 187:7). In any event, when the woman thinks that the blood she saw came out of a wound, she is pure. And even if the blood of the wound was found in an internal bedika during the ona in which her veset is expected to appear, as long as she estimates that the blood came out of a wound and not in the framework of a veset, she is pure. She becomes impure only when she stops supposing that the blood she found came out of the wound, or when she feels the emergence of blood as at the time of the veset, or when she knows from its quantity that it is of a veset.

2) A woman who knows that she has a wound that sometimes releases blood, but she is in doubt whether the blood she saw came out of the wound and is pure, or came out of the womb and is impure: if it was found in an internal bedika during the ona of her fixed veset, she is impure. But if it was found in an internal bedika not during the ona of her fixed veset, or on her white undergarments as a stain, even during the ona of her fixed veset, she is pure (Rema 187:5).

3) A woman who is in doubt whether she has a wound that releases blood or not: if she found blood on a white garment, since the blood came out without a sensation and there is a possibility that perhaps it came out of a wound, she is pure, even if it is larger than a geris, for with stains one attributes leniently. But if she sees blood in an internal bedika, she should be stringent even about any amount. And it is good for her to go and ask a Torah scholar, for perhaps he will be able to know from her question or from the form of the appearance that it is the blood of a wound, regarding which one may be lenient. If the matter recurs, it is preferable that she be examined by a knowledgeable doctor or nurse, and if it is found that she has a wound there that may release blood, from then on she may be lenient regarding an internal bedika not during the ona of her veset (situation 2). And if it is not found that she has a wound that may release blood, her law is like that of other women: in an internal bedika she becomes forbidden by any amount, and with an external appearance according to the rules of the laws of stains.14

notes_en.en:
Nidda 16a: "It was taught: A woman who sees blood due to a wound – even during the days of her nidda – is pure…." And likewise there, 66a: "If she has a wound in that place, she attributes it to her wound… A woman is believed to say: I have a wound in the makor from which blood comes out…." Some say that nowadays one does not attribute to the blood of a wound, just as they were stringent regarding the blood of virginity (Ra'avad and Ramban). However, the overwhelming majority of poskim hold that one should attribute it to the wound and be lenient. There are three situations of a possibility that the blood came out of the wound: 1) When it is clear to the woman that the blood came out of the wound. 2) When it is clear that there is a wound that can release blood, but it is doubtful whether the blood came from it. 3) When it is doubtful whether there is a wound that releases blood. Tosafot wrote (Nidda 16a, s.v. 'u-mar savar'), regarding an internal bedika, that if she felt that the blood came out of her wound, even during the ona of her fixed veset, she is pure (as in the first situation). In addition, the Rema wrote (187:6) that if she says with certainty that this blood is not from the makor, even without a claim that she has a wound that releases blood, she is pure (as in the first situation). But if she did not feel that it is the blood of her wound, even though she also did not feel that it is menstrual blood (as in the second situation), if the internal bedika was carried out during the ona of her fixed veset, she is impure. So wrote the Rema 187:5 and Shakh 26. (In their opinion, a woman who does not have a fixed veset must be stringent in this also during the ona beinonit (the average interval), for otherwise she would never become impure. And it requires further study whether they would say so also when the likelihood that she will see during the ona beinonit is low, or when she saw a small amount of blood that seems to be from a wound and not from a veset.)
Regarding the second situation, in which the woman is in doubt whether the blood is from the wound: some are lenient to attribute it even to a wound that is not known to release blood (Rashba; SA 187:5 according to most Aḥaronim; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 187:46; Be'er Yitzḥak YD 17). And some are stringent to attribute it only to a wound that is known to be able to release blood, but to a wound that is not known to be able to release blood, one does not attribute it (Ha-teruma, Maharam of Rothenburg, Mordekhai, Terumat Ha-deshen). And so ruled many of the Aḥaronim (Shakh 187:24; Noda Bi-Yehuda; Ḥakham Tzvi; Ḥavot Da'at 7; Mishpetei Uziel 2, YD 26; Darkhei Tahara 4:8; Taharat Ha-bayit 5:6). And so one should practice, especially today, when it is possible to be examined by a doctor or nurse and to know whether the wound can release blood.
The third situation is the usual situation of some doubt regarding the existence of a wound: regarding a stain found without a sensation, one should be lenient, and in an internal bedika one should be stringent; and it is good for her to ask a Torah scholar, for perhaps he will find a way to prove that it is from a wound. Sometimes a woman is in doubt whether she is in the first, second or third situation, and then she may ask a Torah scholar, and sometimes, according to what she explains to him, he will know how to answer. She may also be examined by a knowledgeable doctor or nurse. And if even after the examination a doubt remains, with a stain one should be lenient and with a bedika one should be stringent; and when as a result the woman has difficulty becoming pure, she should ask a Torah scholar.
It was further said in Nidda 66a: "And if the blood of her wound differs from the blood of her sighting, she does not attribute it," that is, when the menstrual blood differs from the blood of the wound, and she saw blood in the color of her menstrual blood, one is not lenient. But as long as it is not evident that the blood that came out of her differs from the blood of a wound and resembles her menstrual blood, she attributes it leniently (Rashba, Rosh, Ran and SA 187:1).

sections.body_en:
The blood that renders impure is the blood that comes out of the womb as a result of the regular hormonal activity of the menstrual cycle, or the irregular activity of the blood of ziva. But blood that came out as a result of a wound in the womb does not render impure.

Therefore, a woman who saw blood after the insertion or removal of an 'intrauterine device' – since this procedure may wound the womb or the cervix, this is the blood of a wound, which does not render impure. And if she was in the shiv'a neki'im, she may continue counting them. Likewise, a woman from whose womb growths were removed in a surgical procedure – the blood she sees afterward does not render impure, since it is the blood of a wound. Likewise, a woman who underwent a medical examination that may wound the vagina or the cervix, and saw blood afterward, is pure (more on medical examinations below, 7:7).

Likewise, a woman who was examined by a doctor, and it was found that she has benign or cancerous growths in her womb, on the uterine muscle (a myoma) or on the uterine lining (a polyp), and in the doctor's estimation they may cause bleeding: if she sees blood not at the time of her veset, she is pure. And when she sees blood during the ona of her veset, or estimates that the blood coming out of her is her menstrual blood, she becomes impure.15

A woman who has an 'intrauterine device' in her womb to prevent pregnancy, and after the end of her veset found stains on her white undergarments, is pure.
