For it is known that these devices sometimes wound the womb and cause bleeding, and in the laws of stains one attributes leniently. And if the blood was found in an internal bedika, some are stringent, out of concern that perhaps this bleeding is caused as an inflammatory reaction to the presence of the device in the womb, which causes the breakdown of the lining similar to what happens in a veset, and therefore its law is not like that of the blood of a wound. However, as halakha, after the veset has ended and she has made a hefsek tahara, even if the blood was found in an internal bedika, as long as it is not abundant in the manner of a veset, one may attribute it to blood that came out of a wound caused by the device. However, in order to avoid the doubt, it is proper that a woman who has a device that causes bleeding refrain from performing internal bedikot that are not essential for her purification, and from wearing white underwear (below, 4, note 10).16

notes_en.en:
As we learned in the previous note, the Sages said (Nidda 66a): "A woman is believed to say: I have a wound in the makor from which blood comes out…." The 'makor' is the womb; thus even blood that came out of a wound in the womb does not render impure. So wrote Devar Shmuel 71; Maharam of Lublin 111; Shakh 187:18; 23; Ḥavot Da'at, Ḥiddushim 10 and Bi'urim 4. Even when she has not yet seen that the wound she has releases blood, if other women with such a wound see blood from it, she too may attribute it to her wound (Maharil; Taz 187:10; Ḥokhmat Adam 110:10).
In practice, the removal of growths certainly wounds the womb, and the insertion or removal of an 'intrauterine device' generally wounds it, and likewise there are medical examinations that may wound. Therefore, all the laws we learned in the previous section apply in these cases as well. That is to say, if it is clear to the woman or to the doctor that the blood that came out of her womb is from the wound, even during the ona of her veset it does not render impure, and only when she feels that her menstrual blood is coming out does she become impure (as in situation 1). And if it is not clear that the blood she saw is from the wound, but it is known that she has a wound that can release blood, in an internal bedika during the ona of her veset she is impure, and in an internal bedika not during the ona of her veset, and likewise with stains, she is pure (as in situation 2).
Regarding growths in the womb that cause additional bleeding, a doubt arose whether they create a wound, so that the blood that comes out of it is pure, or whether they trigger a hormonal process that causes bleeding that renders impure (see Sefer PUAH 1:14:6, note 24). It seems that the view of the lenient opinions is correct, for it is not a hormonal action of a veset or of ziva, but rather like the bleeding of a wound. So wrote Tzitz Eliezer 17:37. And so ruled Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and Rav Neuwirth (Nishmat Avraham 187:2:4; Ḥeshev Ha-efod 2:128 was stringent). (According to Rav Dr. Halperin, one should not be lenient in this during the two days adjacent to the veset, before or after it, for if the bleeding appeared close to the veset, it is possible that the growth stretched the uterine lining and caused the menstrual bleeding to come earlier or to last longer.)

Many times the presence of an intrauterine device in the womb causes the veset to be lengthened by several days, and sometimes it even causes bleeding for most of the month. The exact reason for this is not clear. Some say that the presence of the device in the womb causes an inflammatory reaction intended to expel the foreign body, which causes bleeding or a breakdown of the lining that is similar to what happens in a veset, and therefore this bleeding should be forbidden (Nishmat Avraham 194:5:6 in the name of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv and Rav Neuwirth; Be-ohalah Shel Torah 1:24; Rav Yonatan Blass, Teḥumin 31). By contrast, some hold that it is the blood of a wound, and therefore bleeding that is not within the framework of the veset to which that woman was accustomed before the insertion of the device does not render impure (Rav Eliyahu Abergel in Dibrot Eliyahu 6:36; Rav Kafiḥ; and so it emerges from Taharat Ha-bayit 1:5 and p. 267; Rav Dr. Halperin, 'Refu'a, Metzi'ut Ve-halakha' 21). In practice, when it is a stain, one should certainly declare it pure, for with stains the halakha follows the lenient view. However, it seems that even in an internal bedika one may be lenient not during the ona of her veset, since there is a dispute among the doctors whether the blood came out of a wound or from an inflammatory reaction, and even if it is from an inflammatory reaction, it is not clear that its law is like that of menstrual blood and not like that of the blood of a wound. Therefore, since the blood came out without a sensation, one should attribute it to the possibility that perhaps it came out of a wound and does not render impure (as cited above, note 14, and especially according to the view of the Rashba). However, one may be lenient in this on condition that it is clear that the bleeding was caused as a result of the device. For example, before she had a device her veset lasted only six days, and now too she succeeded in making a hefsek tahara at the end of the sixth day and thereby leaving the presumption of impurity; however, unlike what she was accustomed to, during the shiv'a neki'im she found blood in the internal bedika, and it may be assumed that it came because of the device. However, if because of the lengthening of the veset she did not succeed in performing a hefsek tahara, then it is relatively heavy bleeding, and it should be regarded as a continuation of the veset; and only after she makes a hefsek tahara, if she finds blood in the internal bedika beyond the days she was accustomed to see, may she attribute it to a wound caused by the device. Likewise, if after she makes a hefsek tahara she sees a large quantity of blood, such as the blood found toward the end of the veset, one should be stringent, for sometimes most of the menstrual blood comes out continuously, and afterward stops and then resumes coming out until its end.
Regarding a device that contains hormones, some hold that one must be stringent, for perhaps the hormones caused the continued bleeding, since these hormones cause the uterine lining to become thin, and consequently it is more prone to break down, and the bloody material that comes out is from the uterine lining, like the material that comes out in a veset (Rav Dr. Halperin, ibid.; and see Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 5, note 18). However, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that with it too one may be lenient in an internal bedika and attribute the bleeding to a wound, for even though as a result of the hormones the lining becomes thin and prone to bleed, there is still a possibility that the device wounded the womb or triggered an inflammatory reaction that caused bleeding due to a wound, and consequently her law is like that of a woman who has a wound that can release blood, who may be lenient if it is not the time of her veset. This is on condition that it is slight bleeding that cannot be considered a light veset, for sometimes as a result of the hormones there is less blood in the veset. (See above, note 8, regarding stains due to taking hormonal pills.) In any event, a woman who sees stains because of a device or hormonal pills should minimize internal bedikot as much as possible, as I wrote below, 4, note 10.
